lead: A satellite navigation receiver times coded signals from satellites whose orbits it knows, turns each travel time into a range, and solves the ranges together for its position. The receiver's own clock is cheap, so its offset is solved as a fourth unknown. GPS, the American system whose programme name is NAVSTAR, guides airliners, ships and phones, and its timing keeps telecom networks and power grids in step.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for frames and position fixing, and 5.2 for time-based ranging from a point source.

sections.h3: The NAVSTAR constellation and its orbits

blocks.text: GPS is the United States satellite navigation system; its original programme name is NAVSTAR. The baseline design places 24 satellites in 6 orbital planes, each plane inclined at 55° to the equator, at an altitude of about 20,200 km. More satellites are flown than the baseline, so a receiver on the ground usually sees 6 to 12 at a time.

Each satellite moves on a Keplerian ellipse described by six elements: semi-major axis a, eccentricity e, inclination i, right ascension of the ascending node Ω, argument of perigee ω, and the satellite's place on the ellipse. The broadcast ephemeris sends that last one as the mean anomaly at a reference time, plus small correction terms; the receiver works out the true anomaly from it and computes where the satellite was at the instant it transmitted.

blocks.where: T is the orbital period in seconds, a is the semi-major axis in metres and μ = GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² is the Earth's gravitational parameter (the universal constant G times the Earth's mass). With a ≈ 26 560 km, T = 2π √((2.656 × 10⁷)³ ÷ 3.986 × 10¹⁴) ≈ 43 078 s ≈ 11 h 58 min.

blocks.text: That period is half a sidereal day, so after one sidereal day (the Earth turning once) the satellite has made two orbits and is over the same ground point: the ground track and the sky geometry above a site repeat daily, about four minutes earlier each solar day.

sections.h3: PRN codes and the navigation message

blocks.text: All satellites share the same carrier frequencies: L1 at 1575.42 MHz, L2 at 1227.60 MHz and L5 at 1176.45 MHz. They are told apart by code. Each satellite carries its own pseudo-random noise (PRN) sequence, and a receiver separates them by correlating with the right copy — code division multiple access, CDMA.

Two codes ride on L1. The coarse/acquisition (C/A) code runs at 1.023 Mchip/s with 1023 chips, so it repeats every 1 ms. The precision P code runs at 10.23 Mchip/s and repeats weekly; it is encrypted as Y for authorised users. One C/A chip lasts 977.5 ns, 293 m of range; the receiver resolves a small fraction of a chip at the correlation peak.

The navigation message is a 50 bit/s data stream. It carries the satellite's ephemeris, the almanac (coarse orbits of all satellites), clock corrections, ionospheric model coefficients and health flags. A full message takes 12.5 minutes, but one ephemeris set is enough for a first fix.

blocks.where: ρ is the pseudorange in metres, c = 299 792 458 m/s, t<sub>receive</sub> is the arrival time read on the receiver clock and t<sub>transmit</sub> the transmission time read on the satellite clock. Both clocks are imperfect, so ρ is not the true geometric range.

blocks.text: For a satellite at (x<sub>s</sub>, y<sub>s</sub>, z<sub>s</sub>) and a receiver at (x, y, z) the geometric range is r = √((x − x<sub>s</sub>)² + (y − y<sub>s</sub>)² + (z − z<sub>s</sub>)²). The unknowns are x, y, z and the receiver clock offset δt. Each satellite gives one equation, ρ = r + c δt plus small propagation terms.

items: Track four or more satellites and decode each ephemeris.
Compute every satellite position at its transmission time.
Measure code phase and form each pseudorange.
Start from an approximate position and clock offset.
Linearise, solve for the corrections, iterate until they are small.
Output x, y, z, δt and the dilution of precision.

blocks.text: The equations are nonlinear, so the receiver linearises about its guess with a geometry matrix H (one row per satellite: the unit line-of-sight vector and a 1 for the clock), solves Δx = (HᵀH)⁻¹ Hᵀ Δρ, and repeats. The same (HᵀH)⁻¹ gives the dilution of precision (DOP): bunched satellites give a large DOP, which stretches every range error into a bigger position error.

GPS has three segments. The space segment is the satellites. The control segment is a master control station with monitor stations and upload antennas; it tracks the satellites, computes orbit and clock corrections, and uploads them. It also maintains the orbits: the Sun and Moon, the Earth's bulge and sunlight pressure slowly move each satellite out of its slot, so small thruster burns (station-keeping) put it back, with the satellite flagged unhealthy while it manoeuvres. The user segment is every receiver, from a phone to an aircraft GNSS unit.

GLONASS, the Russian Global Navigation Satellite System, flies 24 satellites in 3 planes at about 19 100 km (period about 11 h 15 min), inclined at 64.8° to serve high latitudes; it uses frequency division (FDMA, a different L1 channel near 1602 MHz for each satellite). Galileo (European Union) and BeiDou (China) are also global systems. NavIC is India's regional system: geostationary plus inclined geosynchronous satellites covering India and the surrounding region on L5 and S-band.

Augmentation improves accuracy and integrity. Satellite-based augmentation (SBAS) — GAGAN in India, WAAS in the United States, EGNOS in Europe — broadcasts corrections and integrity flags from a geostationary satellite over a whole region. Ground-based augmentation (GBAS) does the same at one airport for precision approach. Aircraft-based augmentation (ABAS) is receiver monitoring such as RAIM, which checks the ranges against each other.

spec.aria: A straight road from beacon A at 0 to beacon B at 12 kilometres, with the receiver at 5 kilometres. An arrow from A of 5.3 kilometres and an arrow from B of 7.3 kilometres both overshoot the receiver; they overlap by 0.6 kilometres, twice the range bias b. A box gives the equations rho A equals x plus b and rho B equals 12 minus x plus b, so b is 0.3 kilometres, the clock offset is 1.00 microsecond, and x is 5.000 kilometres.

examples.question: A GPS satellite is directly overhead, 20 200 km above a receiver. (a) How long does its signal take to arrive? (b) The receiver clock is fast by 3 µs; what range error does that add to every pseudorange? (c) Why does the receiver need four satellites rather than three?
steps: Data: range R = 20 200 km = 2.0200 × 10⁷ m; c = 299 792 458 m/s; receiver clock offset Δt = 3 µs = 3 × 10⁻⁶ s.
In milliseconds: 0.06738 × 1000 = 67.4 ms, so the signal left the satellite 67.4 ms before it reached the antenna.

A fast receiver clock stamps each arrival 3 µs too late, so every measured travel time looks 3 µs too long and every pseudorange is about 899 m too long: the same error on all of them, which the fourth unknown absorbs.
(c) The unknowns are x, y, z and δt, that is four. Each satellite supplies one equation, so four satellites give four equations. Three would do only if the receiver clock were perfect.
examples.answer: The signal takes 0.0674 s (67.4 ms); the 3 µs clock error adds about 899.4 m (roughly 0.9 km) to every pseudorange; and four satellites are needed because the receiver clock offset is the fourth unknown.

examples.question: A one-dimensional model of the clock problem. Two beacons A and B, synchronised to each other, stand 12.000 km apart on a straight road. A receiver between them has a cheap clock with an unknown offset. Its pseudoranges are ρ<sub>A</sub> = 5.300 km and ρ<sub>B</sub> = 7.300 km. Find the receiver's distance x from A and its clock offset.
steps: Unknowns: x and the range bias b = cδt, which is the same on both readings. True ranges are x from A and 12.000 − x from B.
Equations: ρ<sub>A</sub> = x + b, so 5.300 = x + b; ρ<sub>B</sub> = (12.000 − x) + b, so 7.300 = 12.000 − x + b.
Subtract the second from the first: −2.000 = 2x − 12.000, so x = 5.000 km.
Clock offset δt = b ÷ c = 300 ÷ 299 792 458 = 1.00 µs, fast.
examples.answer: x = 5.000 km from A and the clock is 1.00 µs fast (300 m on each range). Two unknowns needed two beacons; in space there are four unknowns (x, y, z, δt), so four satellites.

traps: Pseudorange is not the geometric range. It carries the receiver clock offset and the propagation delays; writing ρ = r as if the clocks were perfect throws away the reason for the fourth satellite.
Do not mix the carrier with the code. L1 is 1575.42 MHz; the C/A chip rate is 1.023 Mchip/s, exactly 1/1540 of it. One C/A chip is about 293 m, one L1 cycle only 0.19 m.
DOP is geometry, not an error source. It multiplies the range error; it cannot create one, and a low DOP cannot rescue a biased pseudorange.

quiz.q: State the L1 carrier frequency and the C/A code chip rate of GPS.
quiz.a: L1 = 1575.42 MHz; C/A code = 1.023 Mchip/s, with 1023 chips repeating every 1 ms.
Space (the satellites), control (master control, monitor stations, upload antennas) and user (the receivers).

quiz.q: Why does a satellite period of 11 h 58 min give a repeating ground track?
quiz.a: The period is half a sidereal day. In one sidereal day the Earth turns once and the satellite completes two orbits, so it returns over the same ground point and the sky geometry at a fixed site repeats.

quiz.q: Compute the length in metres of one C/A code chip and the travel time it represents.
quiz.a: Chip duration = 1 / (1.023 × 10⁶) s = 977.5 ns. Length = 299,792,458 × 977.5 × 10⁻⁹ = 293.1 m. One chip is about 0.98 µs and 293 m.

quiz.q: Why can one geostationary SBAS satellite such as GAGAN serve India continuously, while the GPS ranging satellites are not geostationary?
quiz.a: SBAS sends corrections and integrity for a wide region, so one fixed satellite can broadcast to the whole region all the time. Ranging satellites must move to give changing geometry and several visible satellites; a geostationary ranger would sit on the equator with poor geometry and no coverage near the poles.

beyond: Not for the exam. Multi-constellation receivers track GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC together, which lowers DOP, and dual-frequency L1/L5 receivers remove most of the ionospheric error. Precise point positioning with correction streams reaches centimetres. Search for multi-GNSS, PPP-RTK and GAGAN.
